bib.title: Learning multiple visual domains with residual adapters

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Learning multiple visual domains with residual adapters", Sylvestre-Alvise Rebuffi, Hakan Bilen, Andrea Vedaldi (VGG, Oxford; Edinburgh). NIPS 2017 (arXiv:1705.08045v5, 27 Nov 2017; first version May 2017).

COVERAGE: I read all 44,217 of 44,217 chars: body, Tables 1 and 2, the full reference list, and Appendix A (per-domain decathlon scores). Nothing was skipped. Figure captions came from figures.py.

**Short answer on priority.** Yes, it comes first for vision. NIPS 2017 / arXiv May 2017 is about two years before Houlsby (ICML 2019). It inserts small residual 1x1-conv "adapter" modules into a ResNet, freezes the shared weights and trains only the adapters (plus BN) for each domain. That is the frozen-backbone, small-inserted-module pattern, but in a CNN rather than a transformer. The paper itself says it was not the only one at the time: "A similar architecture was concurrently proposed in [31]" (Rosenfeld & Tsotsos, arXiv 1705.04228, 2017). It also presents its method as an extension of filter-prediction / low-rank work (Bertinetto et al. 2016). Whether Houlsby cites this paper cannot be checked from this source.

CLAIMS
- claim: A residual adapter is a 1x1 conv bank with an identity skip, so it collapses to the identity when its weights are zero.
  number: none
  setup: inserted into each residual module of a ResNet. BN is folded into the adapter, plus a BN layer before the adapter conv.
  quote: "These modules have the form: g(x;α) =x +α∗x. In order to limit the number of domain-speciﬁc parameters,α is selected to be a bank of 1× 1 ﬁlters. A major advantage of adopting a residual architecture for the adapter modules is that the adapters reduce to the identity function when their coefﬁcients are zero."
  where: p.5, ~char 17,500

- claim: Adapters add about 11% parameters per domain (2x total over ten domains), the backbone is frozen, and the original task suffers no forgetting.
  number: 11% per domain; 2x model
  setup: ResNet28 is pretrained on ImageNet with the adapters in place. The task-agnostic weights are then frozen and the adapters trained on each of 9 other domains.
  quote: "we introduce the residual adapter modules, which increase by 11% the number of parameters per domain, resulting in a 2× model. In the pre-training phase, we ﬁrst pretrain on ImageNet the network with the added modules. Then, we freeze the task agnostic parameters and train the task speciﬁc parameters on the different datasets. Differently from vanilla ﬁne-tuning, there is no forgetting in this setting."
  where: p.8, ~char 31,000

- claim: With weight decay tuned per dataset, adapters match full fine-tuning in mean accuracy and beat it on decathlon score, using 2x parameters instead of 10x.
  number: Res. adapt. decay 76.89 mean / 2621 S, vs Finetune 76.51 / 2500. Res. adapt. finetune all 77.17 / 2643.
  setup: Table 1, top-1 accuracy over 10 Visual Decathlon domains, images at 64x64, ResNet28.
  quote: "Finetune 10× 59.87 60.34 82.12 92.82 55.53 97.53 81.41 87.69 96.55 51.20 76.51 2500" / "Res. adapt. decay 2× 59.67 61.87 81.20 93.88 57.13 97.57 81.67 89.62 96.13 50.12 76.89 2621"
  where: p.7, Table 1

- claim: Placement matters. Fine-tuning only the last two conv layers, at the same 2x parameter budget, does clearly worse than adapters spread through the network.
  number: 64.7% vs 73.9% mean accuracy
  setup: same budget; the authors attribute the gap to overfitting.
  quote: "We also compare to another baseline where we only ﬁnetune the last two convolutional layers and freeze the others ... This model obtains 64.7% mean accuracy over ten datasets, which is signiﬁcantly lower than our 73.9%, likely due to overﬁtting"
  where: p.8, ~char 32,500

- claim: The residual (skip) form beats the same adapter without a skip, and converges faster.
  number: 70.3% vs 73.9%
  setup: the no-skip version equals the low-rank filter parametrization of section 3.1.
  quote: "we also assess the quality of our adapter without residual connections ... this approach achieves an accuracy of 70.3%, which is worse than our 73.9%. We also observe that this conﬁguration requires notably more iterations to converge."
  where: p.8

- claim: Training only BN scale and bias (<0.1% of parameters) already lifts accuracy well above a frozen feature extractor, but it falls short of adapters.
  number: Aircraft 23.31% → 43.05%; BN adapt. mean 71.76 / S 1363
  setup: BN adaptation is the method of Bilen & Vedaldi [5].
  quote: "less than the 0.1% of the model parameters are domain-speciﬁc ... the performances increase very substantially in most cases (e.g. 23.31%→ 43.05% accuracy on Aircraft)."
  where: p.8

- claim: Full fine-tuning and LwF forget ImageNet badly. Adapters keep ImageNet accuracy exactly.
  number: e.g. ImageNet falls to 1.1% after fine-tuning on Aircraft; adapters hold 59.2 throughout
  setup: Table 2, pairwise (ImageNet then one target task). The extraction interleaves the pairs (old, new).
  quote: "Finetune 1.1 60.3 3.6 63.1 0.6 80.3" / "Res. adapt. ﬁnetune all 59.2 63.7 59.2 81.3 59.2 93.3"
  where: p.7, Table 2

- claim: How strongly the adapters are regularized should follow dataset size. Higher decay helps small sets such as Flowers.
  number: decay 0.002 and 0.005 vs default 0.0005
  setup: values from a coarse per-dataset grid search with cross-validation.
  quote: "We also contrast learning the adapter modules with two values of weight decay (0.002 and 0.005) higher than the default 0.0005. ... Using higher decay signiﬁcantly improves the performance on smaller datasets such as Flowers"
  where: p.8

- claim: A single decay for all domains gives a decent mean but a low decathlon score, because Flowers collapses.
  number: 73.88% mean, S 2118; Flowers 66.24
  quote: "although the Res. adapt. model (trained with single decay coefﬁcient for all domains) performs well in terms of average accuracy (73.88%), its decathlon score (2118) is relatively low because the model performs poorly in DTD and Flowers."
  where: p.8

- claim: Domain-specific parameters are about h² (about 9x) fewer than the shared ones in each module.
  number: 2(h²C²+hC) vs 2(C²+5C)
  quote: "the model has 2(h2C2 +hC) domain-agnostic parameters (including biases in the convolutional layers) and 2(C2 + 5C) domain-speciﬁc parameters. ... Hence, there are approximately h2 more domain-agnostic parameters than domain speciﬁc ones (usuallyh2 = 9)."
  where: p.5

- claim: When the domain is unknown, a small predictor network infers it, at little cost.
  number: 99.8% domain accuracy; S 2503
  quote: "obtaining 99.8% accuracy in domain prediction, resulting in a barely noticeable drop in the overall multiple-domain challenge"
  where: p.8

- claim: The paper introduces the Visual Decathlon benchmark: 10 datasets, images resized to a 72px shorter side, a score capped at 10,000, and a baseline error set to twice the fine-tuning error.
  number: 10,000 max; Finetune = 2500 by construction
  quote: "As baseline error rates in eq. (1), we double the error rates of the fully ﬁnetuned networks on each task. In this manner, this 10× model achieves a score of 2,500 points"
  where: p.6 and p.8

LIMITS:
- Every number comes from one run. The paper reports no seeds, no variance and no error bars.
- Decay was chosen by "coarse grid search" on each dataset, so the tuned adapter row gets a tuning advantage the single-setting baselines may not have had.
- The tests use low resolution (64x64 inputs) and a small ResNet28. The authors concede that the gaps to state of the art come from "reduced image resolution (ImageNet, Flower)" and from the UCF dynamic-image representation.
- Adapters are pretrained jointly with ImageNet, so the backbone is not an off-the-shelf frozen model.
- The paper covers CNNs and classification only: no transformers, no language, no VLMs, no detection or segmentation.
- The paper does not measure inference latency, memory or training compute.
- The "finetune all" and "large" (12x) rows are not parameter-efficient.
- The paper names a concurrent near-identical method [31].
- It has dated: the convolutional setting and LoRA-era PEFT have since overtaken it.

BUILDS ON: Bertinetto et al., "Learning feed-forward one-shot learners", NIPS 2016 [2] (low-rank filter prediction; the main base); Jia et al., Dynamic filter networks, NIPS 2016 [16]; Schmidhuber 1992 fast weights [34]; He et al. 2016, identity mappings in ResNets [13]; Zagoruyko & Komodakis 2016, Wide ResNets (ResNet28) [40]; Bilen & Vedaldi 2017, Universal representations (BN adaptation) [5]; Ioffe & Szegedy 2015, BN [15]; Rusu et al. 2016, Progressive nets (tower model) [33]; Li & Hoiem 2016, LwF [21]; concurrent: Rosenfeld & Tsotsos 2017 [31].

CODE: none in the paper. The only formula worth keeping is g(x;α) = x + α∗x, with α a 1x1 filter bank (p.5).

FIGURES:
- Fig. 2 (p.4): "Residual adapter modules. The figure shows a standard residual module with the inclusion of adapter modules (in blue). The filter coefficients (w1, w2) are domain-agnostic and contains the vast majority of the model parameters..." One look at it shows where the adapters sit, which is quicker than reading the text.
- Fig. 1 (p.2): sample images from the 10 decathlon domains. Useful only to show how varied the domains are.

PROBLEMS: Table 2 came out of the extraction with the (old, new) pairs flattened into one row, so it has to be read in alternating pairs. In the equations, ⁄= renders as ≠, and some subscripts and superscripts are garbled ("Emaxd", "h2C2"). The Appendix A table is titled "Table 1" in the extraction, but it holds per-domain decathlon scores. I found no embedded instructions.
